title: Deepavali in Singapore: Little India's 2km Light-Up, Festival Village and What to Do Before Nov 8
excerpt: Serangoon Road's lights run nightly until November 29, the Campbell Lane Festival Village closes on Deepavali itself, and the Indian Heritage Centre's Open House, diya painting and free concerts fill the final week.
body:
• More than 2km of Deepavali lights shine along Serangoon Road in Little India nightly from 7pm to midnight until November 29, organised by the Little India Shop Owners and Heritage Association.
  • Deepavali falls on Sunday, November 8. The Festival Village on Campbell Lane sells clothing, decor, handicrafts and snacks until November 8.
  • Still on this week: Clay Diya Painting at Tekka Place on October 31 (2pm-4pm, free with registration) and Sangeetham Under The Stars, free live music on Campbell Lane on October 31, 8pm-10pm.
  • The Indian Heritage Centre's Deepavali Open House runs until November 8 with heirloom saris, a vintage photo booth and weekend crafts; the Indian Inks pop-up at lyf Farrer Park runs October 31-November 7 with 30+ home-grown brands.

Singapore's Little India is in full Deepavali dress. As part of Deepavali Thiruvizha 2026, organised by the Little India Shop Owners and Heritage Association, more than 2km of lights shine along Serangoon Road nightly, and the diaspora is preparing for the Festival of Lights on Sunday, November 8, Tabla reported. In Campbell Lane, the Festival Village sells traditional clothing, festive decor, handicrafts and snacks — the practical heart of the season for families doing their Deepavali shopping in one evening out.

The light-up and the village

The Little India light-up runs nightly from 7pm to midnight until November 29, and the Festival Village keeps the same hours until November 8. The precinct's Deepavali is one of the largest outside India: the word Deepavali means a "row of lights," and in multicultural Singapore the festival has grown beyond Hindu families into the shared cultural calendar, as SG Indian noted in its guide to this year's celebrations. The wider Deepavali Thiruvizha festivities continue until November 29, with an AR/VR heritage experience, Big Bus Deepavali tours and a photo trail challenge alongside the lights.

What to do before November 8

To make your own festive keepsake, head to Tekka Place. At Clay Diya Painting on October 31, from 2pm to 4pm, free with registration, you can decorate terracotta lamps with acrylic paint, gilding paste and rhinestones. On the same evening, Sangeetham Under The Stars brings free live music to Campbell Lane from 8pm to 10pm — Carnatic classics and fusion sets to Bollywood hits, plus a showcase of emerging artists. Register for workshops at LISHA's ticketing page and check the full programme at deepavali.sg.

The Indian Heritage Centre has turned itself into a "House of Memories" for its annual Deepavali Open House, running until November 8. Its lobby recreates a Deepavali home with archival images of the festival across generations, and three heirloom saris contributed by community members tell family stories of garments kept, worn and handed down. On weekends, visitors can dress up for a retro portrait at a vintage photo booth, paint a clay brooch, or decorate a mini mithai box; ticketed workshops include an Indian miniature painting class (S$28) on October 31 and November 1. The centre, at 5 Campbell Lane, is open 10am to 6pm, Tuesdays to Sundays, until 8pm on Saturdays, with free guided gallery tours at 7pm every Saturday. Details are at the Indian Heritage Centre.

Shop the home-grown pop-up

For festive shopping with a local angle, the Indian Inks Deepavali Pop-up at lyf Farrer Park, 2 Perumal Road, runs October 31 and November 1 (noon to 10pm), November 6 (5pm to 11pm) and November 7 (noon to 10pm), with free admission. What began in 2024 as one weekend with about 12 brands now hosts more than 30, many of them home-based businesses. About 40% of stalls sell clothing, 30% jewellery, and the rest festive bakes, murukku and skincare; henna designs at the Indian Inks booth cost S$10 to S$50 and take five to 20 minutes. For Singapore's Indian community — and for diaspora visitors timing a trip to the festival — the precinct offers the full arc of the season in a few streets: lights, lamps, music, memory and the last-minute shopping run, all before the diyas come out on November 8.
